terms.grammar: nōvī, the perfect of nōscō, with present sense: Nōvī viam; Nōn nōvī viam
evidence: Ter. Ad. 572: sed locum nōvī ubi sit
Ter. Ad. 573: Nōstin’ porticum apud macellum hāc deorsum? — Quid nī nōverim?
terms.comment: Terence’s people use nōvisse for knowing a place and how to get there: Nōvī viam, I know the way; Nōn nōvī viam, I don’t.

evidence: Verg. A. 3.569: ignārīque viae Cyclōpum adlābimur ōrīs
Verg. G. 1.41: ignārōsque viae mēcum miserātus agrestīs
terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica: Verg.; in prose locī ignārus (Sall., Liv.)
terms.comment: In prose, of not knowing the country: locōrum ignārī ab gnārīs circumvenīrentur (Liv. 22.31). For “know one’s way around” a place, locī gnārus: see “familiar”.

phrases.latin: Nōstin’ porticum apud macellum hāc deorsum? — Quid nī nōverim?
phrases.english: Do you know the arcade down this way, by the market? — Of course I know it.

phrases.latin: At nōmen nesciō illīus hominis, sed locum nōvī ubi sit.
phrases.english: I don’t know the man’s name, but I know the place where he is.
and not knowing the way, we drift onto the shores of the Cyclopes
I know the way; follow me.

sources: Lewis & Short: nosco · Lewis & Short: ignarus
Franciscus Morales-Ardaya (Franmorarius), De variis Latinis Graecisque colloquendi formulis (2013), tabula III 12.
